title: Lesson 65 - That Was a Turning Point

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: My draft begins, “I moved from bedside nursing into staff training, and that was a turning point.” It sounds accurate, but also too neat.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Maybe because it starts with the result. What had been happening before the move became possible?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: I had worked on the ward for years, and I used to think the most useful part of my job had to happen beside a patient.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Was that belief already changing before you applied for the training role?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Slowly. New staff would ask me how to organize unfamiliar tasks or how to explain a concern clearly. I would talk through the process, then ask them to explain it back in their own words.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: So teaching was already part of your work, even though it wasn’t in your title.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. By the time a supervisor asked me to help with an orientation session, I had already noticed that I enjoyed making complicated procedures easier to follow.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: What happened in that session?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: One participant asked a question that several people had been avoiding. We changed the example, and the whole room became more willing to speak. That was when I realized training could prevent confusion before it reached a busy shift.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: That sounds like the moment. But did you decide to change jobs immediately?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: No. At the time, I thought leaving the ward might mean giving up the part of nursing that mattered most to me. I had also built routines and relationships there.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: What changed your mind?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: I spoke with people in both roles, observed two more sessions and wrote down what I would gain and what I would miss. The orientation was a turning point, but the decision developed over several months.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: That distinction matters. Otherwise, the story makes one inspiring afternoon look responsible for everything.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. When the coordinator position opened, I applied because I could see a connection between my old experience and the new work. I wasn’t trying to escape one identity and become a completely different person.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: How has the change affected you since then?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It changed the way I define useful work. I still value direct care, but now I also notice what clear preparation can prevent. I ask better questions before building a training session, and I’m less likely to assume that silence means everyone understands.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Looking back, what would you say the turning point really was?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It was the first time I saw teaching as part of the same purpose, not a step away from it. The session opened a possibility; the later conversations, observations and application turned that possibility into a choice.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: That gives you a stronger ending: one moment changed what you could imagine, while the careful steps afterward changed what you actually did.
